How does a computer hear? Sound as a digital wave
Sound is vibration in air. A microphone converts it to an electrical signal, from which successive digital samples are taken.
From a continuous wave to discrete samples
Each point is one sample — the line between them approximates the original wave
The more samples per second, the closer the digital representation is to the original sound.
Sample rate
Measurements per second — speech typically needs sixteen thousand
Bit depth
Precision of each measurement — sixteen bits suffice for speech
Channels
Mono suffices for speech; stereo for music and effects
In summary
Audio is ultimately a sequence of numbers, exactly like an image

Designing voice commands that actually work
A good voice command is short, distinctive and clear in intent — poor design makes the system err constantly.
The rule
Why?
In practice
Acoustically distinct words
Avoid commands that sound alike, such as record and register
Choose clearly different words
Short commands
Long sentences raise the chance of error somewhere in them
Two or three words usually suffice
Confirm before executing
A sensitive command such as delete may be misheard
Ask for spoken confirmation before executing
An always-available alternative
Noise or accent may block recognition
Provide a manual button for every voice command

Limits of speech recognition: what to expect
Ambient noise
Background sound sharply reduces accuracy in open environments
Accents and terminology
Models are mostly trained on standard speech and err on regional accents
Proper nouns
Personal names and technical terms are frequently wrong
Punctuation and diacritics
The produced text needs human review before official use
The rule: show the produced text to the user for review before saving — never write it straight into an official record.

Secure connection from PHP and preventing SQL injection
❌ Dangerous: concatenating input directly
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" . $_POST['name'] . "'"
A malicious user types: ' OR '1'='1 and obtains all the data without a valid password.
✅ Safe: prepared statements
$stmt = $pdo->prepare(
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?"
);
$stmt->execute([$_POST['name']]);
The ? is a placeholder for a value only — it can never become an SQL command, whatever the user types.
The rule: never concatenate user input into SQL text — always use PDO or mysqli with prepared statements.

Inference engine — 1: Forward chaining
Forward Chaining
We start from known facts, fire every rule whose conditions hold, add its conclusion as a new fact, and repeat until no rule can fire.
Initial facts
▶
R1 fires
▶
R2 fires
▶
Final conclusion
Data-driven: suited to continuous monitoring — "what can we conclude from everything we know now?"
Worked example

R2: initially eligible + service > 1 year ⇒ eligible for leave
R3: eligible for leave + sufficient balance ⇒ ✅ approved

Backward Chaining
We start from a goal we want to prove and work backwards to the facts that establish it — this is what a system does when it asks you specific questions.

▲ requires
Approved?
Urgent request? — a fact
▲ requires

The essential difference
Direction
forward from facts  ⇔  backward from the goal
Best use
continuous monitoring  ⇔  a specific query
Computational efficiency
may check unnecessary rules  ⇔  checks only what concerns the goal

When rules conflict
What if two rules apply at once with contradictory conclusions? This is rule conflict, and it has three resolution strategies.
Priority
Priority
Each rule carries a preset priority — the highest fires on conflict
Specificity
Specificity
The more specific rule — with more conditions — is preferred over the general one
Order
Ordering
The first rule whose conditions hold fires, following list order
⚖️ Example: a general rule "all requests are processed within 3 days" and a more specific one "urgent requests are processed within an hour" — the second wins by specificity.

The very strength that grants transparency also brings brittleness when a case falls outside expectations.

A single case outside the written rules can confuse the system entirely — even one perfectly obvious to any human.

How do language models work? — 2 Prediction
The core of the model is surprisingly simple: it predicts the most likely next token — then repeats that thousands of times.
Input sentence:
"The administrative capital of the country is ..."
Probabilities the model computes:
City A
78%
City B
14%
City C
5%
Two important consequences
1. The model does not "know" the answer — it selects the statistically most likely one.
2. Because the choice is probabilistic, the answer may differ each time you ask the same question — this is called non-determinism.
Herein lies both the secret of its power and of its error.

Root cause
The model is built to produce likely text — not to verify truth. When it does not know, it does not stay silent; it generates what "resembles" a correct answer.
Inventing references and book titles that do not exist
Producing links that look valid but do not work
Attributing a quote to someone who never said it
High confidence in phrasing despite wrong content

Ask the question two ways
